author: claude
title: Blind Tasting: Deductive Logic from Color to Variety

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: In blind tasting, you try a wine without knowing what it is. How do professionals guess the grape and region so well?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It's not magic. It's deductive tasting. You collect clues step by step and slowly remove the impossible answers.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: With the eyes. The color hue gives the first clues. A pale, light red might suggest a thin-skinned grape like Pinot Noir. A deep, almost black color could point to Syrah or Cabernet Sauvignon.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes. Fruit character helps a lot. Red fruits like cherry suggest one group of grapes, black fruits like blackcurrant suggest another. Oak, earth or herbal notes add more clues about winemaking and age.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's where structural markers are important. Acidity, tannin, alcohol and body. For example, high acidity and fine tannins with red fruit often suggest a cool climate. Ripe fruit with high alcohol suggests a warmer region.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. You might say: light color, high acidity, red fruit, earthy notes, light tannin. That points toward Pinot Noir from a cool region, maybe Burgundy. You make a logical conclusion, even if you're not one hundred percent sure. And when you're wrong, you learn the most.
